articles.title: The Monitor That Only Passed When It Won a Race
articles.excerpt: A browser monitor I was migrating failed about two runs in every three. The rest passed cleanly. The application behind it was healthy. Nobody could see a pattern. The run history for that stretch was…
articles.body: A browser monitor I was migrating failed about two runs in every three. The rest passed cleanly. The application behind it was healthy. Nobody could see a pattern. The run history for that stretch was 67 runs. 25 passed. 42 failed. That is a 37.3% pass rate on a monitor watching an application that was working. This post is about how that failure was found and fixed. The fix itself was small. The idea behind it is the part worth keeping: A check that passes only when it wins a race is not a passing check. Why intermittent failures are the hardest kind A monitor that always fails is easy. You look at it, find the broken thing, and fix it. A monitor that fails sometimes is harder, for three reasons. It teaches people to ignore it. After a week of flapping, a red run stops meaning anything.

articles.title: containerd 2.2's mount manager panics on a one-mount mkfs chain
articles.excerpt: containerd 2.2 shipped a mount manager: a service that can format a file as ext4 or xfs, attach it as a loopback device, and hand the result to a runtime, all from a single Activate call instead of th…
articles.body: containerd 2.2 shipped a mount manager: a service that can format a file as ext4 or xfs, attach it as a loopback device, and hand the result to a runtime, all from a single Activate call instead of the usual truncate , mkfs , losetup , mount sequence. I wanted to know whether that call is actually faster than doing it by hand, so I wrote a small Go program against the manager's package directly and ran both paths three times each on the same machine. The manual sequence came out at 23.5 to 25.9 milliseconds. The mount manager's Activate came out at 29.6 to 47.2 milliseconds. It was not faster. Along the way it also panicked once, leaked a raw BoltDB error once, and left a loop device attached with nothing able to find it again.

articles.title: AWS Lambda Durable Functions and the Replay Bug in Human-in-the-Loop Agents
articles.excerpt: Ciao 👋 Here is a sentence that should not be possible: my workflow executed an action a human explicitly did not approve. Not a different user's action, not a race condition, not a bug in my business…
articles.body: Ciao 👋 Here is a sentence that should not be possible: my workflow executed an action a human explicitly did not approve. Not a different user's action, not a race condition, not a bug in my business logic. The human looked at the screen, saw "refund," clicked approve, and the system went and did "escalate" instead. Nobody tampered with anything. The code looked correct. The culprit was a feature I had just started using and did not fully understand: AWS Lambda durable functions, and the one thing about them that will quietly wreck you if you miss it. This is the story of building a human-in-the-loop agent workflow, watching it betray the human, and the one-line structural fix that stops it. Everything here runs locally with no AWS account, and I deployed it to real Lambda too.

articles.title: I used to love foldable phones. Now, I can’t stand them
articles.excerpt: It turns out I’d rather keep my phone and tablet apart.
articles.body: Just as they have with their inner screens, foldables have divided the user base into two camps — either you find regular phones too simplistic to go back to, or you just don’t want to see your phone fold in half anymore. There is no other realization you have after living with a foldable. And the title must’ve given away that I fall under the second category. I used to be a book-style foldable die-hard, but as the novelty wore off, its flaws became glaring by the day. And no, I’m not concerned by foldables coming with one less rear camera or a more fragile exterior. My problem is more fundamental. I just can’t fathom the very idea of a device deploying complicated and delicate (not to mention expensive) mechanics to do two things at once when I’m not convinced it excels at either.
